paragraphs: The paper studies optimization problems in which an upper-level decision depends on an equilibrium among lower-level participants. These problems also describe Stackelberg games with multiple followers. Their nested structure makes them difficult to solve: even calculating a first derivative can require differentiating through the lower-level response, creating a substantial computational burden.

The authors replace this hierarchy with two bounding problems: a T-step Cournot game and a T-step monopoly model. The Cournot construction provides an upper bound, while the monopoly construction provides a lower bound. Both are ordinary equilibrium or optimization problems that can be addressed efficiently using first-order methods, avoiding differentiation across the original hierarchy.

For a wide range of problems, increasing T can make these bounds arbitrarily tight. Under appropriate conditions, the authors also show that a small T usually provides a practically acceptable approximation. Numerical examples illustrate the analysis. The contribution is a way to control approximation quality through simpler bounding problems, with the usefulness of small T depending on the stated conditions.
icml-2023-achieving-hierarchy-free-appro.tldr: Two simpler bounding problems can approximate difficult bilevel equilibrium programs increasingly closely without differentiating through their hierarchy.

paragraphs: Masked image modeling trains a vision model by hiding part of an image and asking it to reconstruct the missing content. Although this approach has worked well with vision transformers, its underlying mechanism has remained unclear. The paper also challenges earlier claims that the approach is incompatible with convolutional neural networks.

The authors observe that masked reconstruction helps models learn better middle-order interactions among image patches. This focuses attention on relationships involving groups of patches as a source of more generalizable features. That interpretation motivates A²MIM, a unified masked image modeling framework designed to work with both transformers and convolutional networks.

Experiments on popular benchmarks show improved learned representations and stronger transfer to downstream vision tasks. These findings support the usefulness of the proposed framework across the two architecture families considered. The broader contribution connects an account of what masked reconstruction teaches with a practical pretraining method, making the technique applicable beyond the transformer setting in which it had achieved prominent success.
icml-2023-architecture-agnostic-masked-i.tldr: A²MIM uses an interpretation of masked reconstruction as learning patch interactions to support pretraining both transformers and convolutional networks.

paragraphs: BLIP-2 addresses the expense of training large vision-and-language systems end to end. It starts with an already trained image encoder and an already trained large language model, keeping both frozen. The learning effort instead centers on a lightweight Querying Transformer that connects visual information with the language model’s capabilities.

This connecting component is pretrained in two stages. The first develops vision-language representations using the frozen image encoder. The second develops image-to-language generation using the frozen language model. Splitting the process this way provides a route to combining existing models while training substantially fewer parameters than methods that update larger portions of the system.

The paper reports state-of-the-art results across various vision-language tasks. On zero-shot VQAv2, BLIP-2 outperforms Flamingo80B by 8.7% while using 54 times fewer trainable parameters. It also demonstrates emerging image-to-text generation abilities that follow natural-language instructions without task-specific examples. These results show that learning the connection between frozen components can deliver strong performance with a much smaller trainable component.
icml-2023-blip-2-bootstrapping-language-.tldr: BLIP-2 connects frozen vision and language models through a lightweight transformer, achieving strong vision-language results with far fewer trainable parameters.

paragraphs: Anomaly detection can benefit from expert feedback, but a limited labeling budget makes the choice of examples important. The paper studies how to select informative data for feedback and then use those labels to improve detection. Its motivating settings include medical diagnostics and fraud detection, where identifying unusual cases is a central task.

The authors first establish theoretical conditions under which anomaly scores learned from queried, labeled examples generalize to unlabeled data. Guided by this analysis, they propose a labeling strategy that achieves optimal data coverage under the budget constraint. Coverage provides the link between choosing which examples receive labels and extending the resulting information to the remaining data.

The paper also introduces a learning framework for semi-supervised anomaly detection, combining labeled and unlabeled data. Extensive experiments cover images, tabular records, and video, with reported state-of-the-art performance under labeling constraints. The findings support treating label selection and detector learning as connected design decisions: the limited feedback is useful both because of which examples are selected and how the learning framework uses them.
icml-2023-deep-anomaly-detection-under-l.tldr: The paper combines coverage-based label selection with semi-supervised anomaly detection to improve performance under limited labeling budgets.

paragraphs: Concentration inequalities describe how strongly random quantities cluster around their typical behavior. They provide tools for analyzing statistical estimates and learning procedures. This paper develops McDiarmid-type exponential inequalities for functions with unbounded interactions, extending the available analysis to settings where the relevant effects cannot simply be treated as bounded.

The results cover three distribution classes: sub-Gaussian, sub-exponential, and heavy-tailed. For the first two classes, the proposed inequalities depend on the distribution, distinguishing them from the recent results discussed by the authors. For heavy-tailed distributions, the paper supplies inequalities that the authors identify as unavailable in previous work. These are separate contributions within the same concentration framework.

The paper illustrates the inequalities through applications to the sample mean, U-statistics, and V-statistics. These examples connect the mathematical bounds to concrete statistical quantities rather than leaving them as abstract statements about random functions. The significance is a broader set of tools for studying concentration under different distributional behaviors, including heavy tails, with the relevant distribution class remaining part of the result.
icml-2023-distribution-dependent-mcdiarm.tldr: The paper extends McDiarmid-type concentration bounds to unbounded interactions across sub-Gaussian, sub-exponential, and heavy-tailed distributions.

paragraphs: The paper studies how to locate times when the statistical behavior of a high-dimensional time series changes. Many features can make accurate change-point estimation computationally demanding. The proposed Divide and Conquer Dynamic Programming framework, or DCDP, aims to preserve strong localization accuracy while substantially reducing the computation needed to obtain it.

DCDP uses a class of greedy algorithms applicable to a broad variety of high-dimensional statistical models and capable of almost linear computational complexity. The authors analyze three settings: changes in a mean model, a Gaussian graphical model, and a linear regression model. For each, they derive non-asymptotic accuracy bounds, describing estimation performance at finite sample sizes.

The analysis establishes consistent change-point estimation with sharp rates that are optimal in some cases. The procedures also incur substantially lower computational costs than the best available algorithms considered by the authors. Experiments on synthetic and real data support these findings. Together, the results show that the framework can combine computational savings with rigorous accuracy guarantees across several distinct forms of high-dimensional change.
icml-2023-divide-and-conquer-dynamic-pro.tldr: DCDP combines almost linear computation with strong change-point localization guarantees across three high-dimensional statistical settings.

paragraphs: Quantum optimal control asks how to choose a control variable so that a physical quantity is maximized at a specified final time. The system evolves according to a time-dependent Schrödinger equation, linking the optimization objective to quantum dynamics. This paper presents quantum algorithms for the problem and reports an exponential speed advantage over classical algorithms.

The algorithms combine time-dependent Hamiltonian simulation with fast gradient estimation. Simulation handles the system’s evolving dynamics, while gradient estimation supports the search for a better control. This combination connects the physical evolution being controlled to the optimization procedure, making both parts central to the proposed computational improvement.

The authors also analyze errors from representing the control function in finite dimensions, discretizing the Schrödinger equation, numerical quadrature, and optimization. Accounting for these contributions provides a total-error analysis across the algorithm’s stages. The hardware requirement is explicit: the algorithms need fault-tolerant quantum computers. Their stated advantage therefore concerns computation with that capability, alongside an analysis of how approximation errors accumulate through the solution process.
icml-2023-efficient-quantum-algorithms-f.tldr: The paper presents quantum optimal-control algorithms with a stated exponential speedup, comprehensive error analysis, and a requirement for fault-tolerant quantum hardware.

paragraphs: Federated learning lets clients train locally for several steps before a server combines their updates. The paper examines adversarial training in this setting, where repeated local updates and differences between clients complicate both robustness and mathematical analysis. It formulates a general federated adversarial learning framework adapted from centralized adversarial learning.

Each client runs an inner loop that generates adversarial examples and an outer loop that updates its model using adversarial training. The server aggregates the updates and broadcasts the combined model. A global robust loss expresses this process as a min-max problem, connecting the generation of challenging inputs with the effort to reduce the model’s resulting loss.

The convergence analysis uses gradient approximation and coupling techniques to handle the nested optimization, local updates, and client heterogeneity. In the over-parameterized regime, the authors show that the minimum loss attained by the algorithm can become epsilon-small with chosen learning rates and communication rounds. The analysis accommodates non-identically distributed clients, extending the theoretical account to heterogeneous federated data under the stated regime.
icml-2023-federated-adversarial-learning.tldr: A federated adversarial-training framework receives convergence guarantees in an over-parameterized regime that allows heterogeneous client data.

paragraphs: In vertical federated learning, different clients hold different features of the training data. A split model distributes its computation between those clients and a central server. This arrangement creates two problems addressed by the paper: slow clients can degrade training performance, and the embeddings clients upload can expose information about their private data or models.

FedVS introduces secret-sharing schemes for both local data and local models. The schemes allow the aggregate of all clients’ embeddings to be reconstructed losslessly from computation shares supplied by clients that are not straggling. This makes the reconstruction of the required aggregate central to both maintaining training progress and protecting the information held by participants.

The paper guarantees information-theoretic privacy against colluding clients and a curious server within its scheme. Experiments span tabular, computer-vision, and multi-view datasets, reporting advantages over baseline protocols in straggler mitigation and privacy protection. The contribution brings these two concerns into one design: privacy-preserving shared computation also supplies the mechanism for recovering the aggregate despite straggling clients.
icml-2023-fedvs-straggler-resilient-and-.tldr: FedVS uses secret sharing to protect split-model federated learning while recovering exact embedding aggregates despite straggling clients.

paragraphs: GraphCleaner addresses incorrect node labels in graph datasets, a data-quality problem that has received less attention than labeling errors in images or text. Such errors affect how learning systems are developed and evaluated. The paper proposes a post-hoc method for detecting and correcting mislabeled nodes by using information available in the graph.

The method combines synthetic examples of realistic labeling mistakes with neighborhood-aware detection. It uses dependencies among neighboring nodes in both their labels and a base classifier’s predictions. This allows the detection process to consider the surrounding graph context when assessing a node’s label, while synthetic mislabels supply examples of the errors it aims to recognize.

Across six datasets and six experimental settings, GraphCleaner improves on the closest baseline by an average of 0.14 in F1 and 0.16 in MCC. Case studies uncover previously unknown problems in PubMed, Cora, CiteSeer, and OGB-arxiv. At least 6.91% of PubMed is identified as mislabeled or ambiguous; removing the identified data raises reported evaluation performance from 86.71% to 89.11%.
icml-2023-graphcleaner-detecting-mislabe.tldr: GraphCleaner combines synthetic labeling errors and graph-neighborhood information to detect mislabels, including previously unknown problems in widely used benchmarks.

paragraphs: Long-horizon offline decision making must learn extended behavior from existing data, where limited examples, sparse rewards, and accumulating variance can complicate learning. This paper frames the task as conditional generation. It incorporates goals into control-as-inference graphical models, establishing a basis for generating plans through a hierarchy of goals and actions.

The proposed HDMI method uses a cascade of diffusion models with classifier-free guidance. A reward-conditioned goal diffuser discovers subgoals, and a goal-conditioned trajectory diffuser generates the corresponding action sequences. This division lets the system model which intermediate goals to pursue separately from the trajectories used to carry them out, while connecting the two through conditioning.

The method also uses planning-based subgoal extraction to address suboptimal data and transformer-based diffusion to handle long-range dependencies among subgoals. Numerical experiments report advantages over state-of-the-art offline reinforcement learning methods and conditional generative models on long-horizon tasks. The findings support the proposed combination of hierarchical generation and goal conditioning as an effective approach in the evaluated decision-making settings.
icml-2023-hierarchical-diffusion-for-off.tldr: HDMI uses a hierarchy of goal and trajectory diffusion models to improve long-horizon offline decision making.

paragraphs: The paper asks whether reinforcement learning needs more samples simply because an episode lasts longer. Earlier treatments impose reward assumptions that can complicate comparisons or restrict observation noise. The authors introduce expected boundedness: the expected total reward is bounded, while the realized reward sum need not obey the stricter almost-sure bound used in earlier work.

Under this relaxation, they develop a generic algorithm for both Markov decision processes and games. It reduces the original problem to a well-conditioned auxiliary Markovian environment that preserves only important state-action pairs. This construction provides the basis for obtaining sample-complexity guarantees without dependence on the episode horizon.

The algorithm requires roughly S²A divided by epsilon² episodes, up to suppressed logarithmic factors, to obtain an epsilon-optimal policy or strategy with high probability through interaction with the auxiliary environment. Here S and A count states and actions. The result broadens horizon-free guarantees to stochastic rewards under expected boundedness, while retaining an explicit accuracy-dependent sample bound and allowing the game setting as well.
icml-2023-horizon-free-learning-for-mark.tldr: An auxiliary-environment reduction yields horizon-independent episode bounds for decision processes and games with bounded expected total rewards.

paragraphs: Showing that a transformer can represent a useful computation does not establish that training will discover it. This paper investigates that gap for topic structure, treating semantic structure as patterns of word co-occurrence. The goal is to explain how learning produces topic-sensitive representations inside the embedding and self-attention layers.

The authors combine mathematical analysis with experiments using Wikipedia and synthetic data generated through Latent Dirichlet Allocation. They identify two signatures of learned topic structure. Words belonging to the same topic have higher average inner products between their embeddings, and pairs of same-topic words receive higher average attention from one another.

These findings connect an observable property of the data to specific quantities within a transformer, providing a more detailed account than task performance alone. The mathematical analysis relies on several assumptions introduced to make the problem tractable, which the authors check on data. The result therefore offers a qualified mechanistic explanation of topic learning, supported by both analysis and experiments, rather than an unrestricted account of every form of semantic learning.
icml-2023-how-do-transformers-learn-topi.tldr: Analysis and experiments show how transformer embeddings and attention encode word-topic structure through stronger average same-topic relationships.

paragraphs: Individual fairness expresses the idea that similar people should receive similar treatment. Existing approaches often pursue this by requiring predictions to remain stable when sensitive information is perturbed. The paper argues that these perturbations can ignore feature correlations and inherent data constraints, causing training to focus on unrealistic examples outside the data’s natural structure.

The authors propose learning to generate antidote data that approximately follows the data distribution. These examples are intended to counter individual unfairness while respecting the structure that conventional adversarial perturbations may overlook. The generated data can accompany the original training set in a generic optimization procedure, making the approach usable as preprocessing.

The same antidote data can also be integrated with distributionally robust optimization during training. Experiments on multiple tabular datasets report improved resistance to individual unfairness with minimal or no loss of predictive utility relative to baselines. The findings support realistic data generation as a practical route to fairness, with two integration options and an empirical tradeoff between fair treatment and predictive performance.
icml-2023-learning-antidote-data-to-indi.tldr: Generated antidote examples approximately follow the data distribution and reduce individual unfairness with minimal or no predictive cost in the reported experiments.

paragraphs: Online bipartite matching requires irreversible decisions as information about new items arrives. Applications include online advertising. Expert algorithms can offer worst-case guarantees but may disappoint on average, while reinforcement learning can improve typical performance yet behave arbitrarily poorly. The paper develops LOMAR to combine learned decisions with protection supplied by an expert algorithm.

For each arriving item, LOMAR decides whether to follow the expert or the reinforcement learning policy. Its switching condition accounts for uncertainty about future arrivals. The learned policy is trained with this switching operation explicitly included, so training reflects the decision process that will actually determine which matches are made.

The authors prove that, for any chosen rho between zero and one, LOMAR is rho-competitive against the supplied expert algorithm. The guarantee is therefore relative to that expert, with rho specifying the protected comparison. Experiments demonstrate advantages over existing baselines. Together, the theory and empirical results support improving average matching performance while maintaining a quantified worst-case relationship to an expert’s performance.
icml-2023-learning-for-edge-weighted-onl.tldr: LOMAR switches between learned and expert matching decisions to improve average performance while preserving a tunable guarantee relative to the expert.

paragraphs: Large transformer models can demand substantial memory and computation, motivating methods that compress their learned weights. LoSparse approximates a weight matrix as the sum of a low-rank matrix and a sparse matrix. This combines two compression strategies within a single representation, allowing each component to preserve a different aspect of the original weights.

The low-rank component compresses coherent, expressive structure across neurons. Pruning removes incoherent, less expressive portions, while the retained sparse component contributes diversity beyond the low-rank approximation. The authors describe these roles as complementary: low-rank approximation helps prevent excessive loss of expressive neurons, and pruning enriches what can be represented alongside the low-rank structure.

The method is evaluated on natural-language understanding, question answering, and language generation tasks. The paper reports significant improvements over existing compression methods across these evaluations. The findings support combining shared structure and sparse retained information when compressing transformers. The central contribution is the joint approximation itself and the way its two parts are designed to compensate for weaknesses of using either strategy alone.
icml-2023-losparse-structured-compressio.tldr: LoSparse compresses transformer weights with complementary low-rank and sparse components, outperforming existing compression methods in the reported language-task evaluations.

paragraphs: Policy optimization directly learns how an agent should act, but its flexibility can come with slow convergence and high sample requirements. Earlier sample-efficiency advances had mainly covered tabular or linear settings. This paper develops LPO, a low-switching policy optimization algorithm that extends the analysis to general nonlinear function approximation.

LPO draws on tools developed for value-based learning, including bounded eluder dimension and online sensitivity sampling. These tools help organize exploration and control the complexity relevant to learning. The analysis expresses sample requirements through a function-class complexity measure d and the desired suboptimality gap epsilon, connecting the guarantee to both approximation complexity and target accuracy.

The algorithm obtains an epsilon-optimal policy with a sample bound proportional to a polynomial in d divided by epsilon cubed, up to logarithmic factors. This improves the previously best-known epsilon-to-the-eighth dependence cited for policy optimization. Experiments with deep neural networks also show benefits from the theoretical ideas. The contribution combines a sharper sample guarantee under the analyzed complexity framework with empirical evidence for its design principles.
icml-2023-low-switching-policy-gradient-.tldr: LPO extends sample-efficient policy optimization to nonlinear approximation and improves the stated accuracy dependence from epsilon⁻⁸ to epsilon⁻³.

paragraphs: Physics-informed neural networks can solve partial differential equations by dividing a domain into regions and assigning a network to each region. Conditions at the interfaces connect these regional solutions, but performance depends strongly on their selection. METALIC learns how to choose appropriate interface conditions across a family of parameterized equations.

The method uses contextual multi-armed bandits, with equation parameters providing context for condition selection. One version maintains a Gaussian-process reward model that predicts performance from the parameters and candidate conditions throughout training. The authors prove sublinear regret bounds for upper-confidence-bound and Thompson-sampling strategies, giving theoretical support to this adaptive selection process.

A second version separates training into stochastic and deterministic phases, maintaining a reward model for each. This allows different interface conditions at different stages instead of requiring one selection throughout the entire process. Experiments on four benchmark equation families demonstrate advantages for METALIC. The contribution makes interface selection responsive to both the equation being solved and, in the two-stage version, the phase of training.
icml-2023-meta-learning-of-interface-con.tldr: METALIC uses contextual bandits to adapt interface conditions for multi-domain physics-informed networks across equations and training stages.

paragraphs: Online kernel regression must balance predictive performance against computational cost as data arrives. The paper proposes AOGD-ALD and NONS-ALD, which retain nearly optimal regret bounds with sublinear computational complexity under sufficient conditions. Regret measures accumulated loss relative to a comparison predictor, making this a tradeoff between prediction quality and the work required to maintain it.

Both algorithms maintain a changing collection of nearly orthogonal basis elements to approximate the kernel mapping. Controlling approximation error preserves their regret guarantees. The required basis size depends on the allowed error and how quickly the kernel matrix’s eigenvalues decay, linking computational savings to the structure of the kernel problem.

With exponential eigenvalue decay, both achieve O(log² T) computation: AOGD-ALD has O(√L(f)) regret, while NONS-ALD has O(d_eff(μ) log T) regret. For polynomial decay, the same respective bounds accompany sublinear computation when p > 4 and p ≥ 10. L(f) is comparator cumulative loss and d_eff is effective dimension. The regret bounds are nearly optimal but not comparable, so neither uniformly dominates the other.
icml-2023-nearly-optimal-algorithms-with.tldr: Two adaptive kernel approximations achieve nearly optimal, distinct regret bounds with sublinear computation under sufficient eigenvalue-decay conditions.

paragraphs: Nyström approximation reduces a large kernel matrix to a lower-rank representation, making kernel methods more manageable at scale. However, earlier optimality analyses often assume that the target regression function belongs exactly to the learner’s hypothesis space. This paper studies the agnostic setting, which allows the target to fall outside that space.

The authors provide a refined generalization analysis showing that Nyström methods can still achieve optimal rates that depend on the hypothesis space’s capacity. With standard uniform sampling, they establish these guarantees for some agnostic settings. This demonstrates that a mismatch between the target and the hypothesis space does not automatically prevent optimal convergence.

Using data-dependent sampling, including leverage-score sampling, the analysis extends capacity-dependent optimal rates across the whole agnostic range considered. The authors identify this full-range result as a first for Nyström approximation. The distinction between sampling methods matters: uniform sampling supports part of the range, while data-dependent selection supports the broader guarantee. The contribution clarifies how approximation and sampling interact when the target is not exactly representable.
icml-2023-optimal-convergence-rates-for-.tldr: Nyström kernel learning can achieve capacity-dependent optimal rates even outside the hypothesis space, with data-dependent sampling covering the full agnostic range analyzed.

paragraphs: Propensity-based weighting is used to reduce bias in recommendation, but learning propensities raises a further question: how should their quality be judged? The paper examines whether commonly used metrics, including the pursuit of smaller cross-entropy loss, adequately reflect their usefulness for debiasing. It focuses on the balancing behavior that the learned propensities produce.

The authors introduce balanced mean squared error, or BMSE, as a metric for this purpose. Building on it, they propose IPS-V2 and DR-V2 loss estimators. Their theoretical analysis shows stronger propensity balancing and lower variance without an additional bias cost, connecting the proposed evaluation criterion to improvements in the estimators used for learning.

The paper also develops a co-training method that learns balanced representations together with unbiased predictions. Experiments use three real-world datasets, including a large industrial dataset, and report improved balancing and debiasing performance. The findings connect three parts of the recommendation pipeline: how propensity quality is measured, how weighted loss is estimated, and how representations and predictions are learned together.
icml-2023-propensity-matters-measuring-a.tldr: A balancing-focused propensity metric leads to revised estimators and co-training that improve debiasing in the reported recommendation experiments.

paragraphs: Backdoor attacks implant unwanted behavior in neural networks, creating a need to identify and remove the neurons associated with that behavior. Reconstructive Neuron Pruning, or RNP, approaches this through a deliberate unlearning-and-recovery process. It uses a small collection of clean samples to expose backdoor-related neurons before pruning them.

The first stage increases the model’s error on the clean samples to unlearn at the neuron level. The second reduces error on those same samples, but performs recovery at the filter level. This asymmetry is the central design choice: the two stages operate at different levels of the network while using the same clean data.

The authors show that this procedure can expose and prune backdoor neurons from a wide range of attacks using only a few clean samples, reporting state-of-the-art defense performance. They also find that the intermediate unlearned model can improve backdoor removal, trigger recovery, backdoor label detection, and backdoor sample detection. The intermediate stage therefore supplies useful information beyond its role in the final pruning procedure.
icml-2023-reconstructive-neuron-pruning-.tldr: RNP exposes backdoor neurons by unlearning at the neuron level and recovering at the filter level before pruning.

paragraphs: Federated learning commonly combines client models using weights proportional to local dataset sizes and normalized to sum to one. This paper revisits both choices. It finds that allowing the sum to fall below one shrinks the global model’s weights, producing an effect analogous to weight decay that can improve generalization.

The authors investigate how client data heterogeneity and the number of local training epochs affect the optimal amount of shrinking. They also study the relative weights assigned to individual clients through a notion called client coherence. Their analysis identifies a critical point in training, before which more coherent clients have a more important role in generalization.

These observations motivate FedLAW, which learns aggregation weights instead of relying solely on the conventional fixed rule. Extensive experiments across different datasets and models report large improvements in global-model generalization. The contribution separates two aspects of aggregation that normalization ordinarily ties together: the overall scale of the combined model and the relative influence of each participating client.
icml-2023-revisiting-weighted-aggregatio.tldr: FedLAW learns federated aggregation weights using insights about global weight shrinking and the changing importance of coherent clients.

paragraphs: Transformer Hawkes processes model sequences of events, including their types and arrival times. Existing likelihood-based training involves an intractable integral, and the methods discussed in the paper do not quantify predictive uncertainty. SMURF-THP addresses both issues by changing the learning objective and using the learned model to generate possible arrival times.

The method learns the score function for event arrival time through score matching, avoiding the troublesome likelihood computation. The learned score then enables sampling from the predictive arrival-time distribution. Multiple generated arrival times provide the basis for confidence intervals, turning a distribution of possible outcomes into an explicit measure of timing uncertainty.

Experiments examine event-type prediction and uncertainty in arrival times. Across all reported experiments, SMURF-THP achieves better confidence calibration than existing likelihood-based methods while maintaining comparable prediction accuracy. This matters because accurate predictions and informative confidence are separate properties. The reported results show improved uncertainty estimates without sacrificing comparable predictive performance, with the same score-based formulation supporting both training and uncertainty quantification.
icml-2023-smurf-thp-score-matching-based.tldr: SMURF-THP learns event-arrival scores to avoid intractable likelihood computation and produce better-calibrated uncertainty with comparable prediction accuracy.

paragraphs: Perception metrics borrowed from computer vision do not fully describe how perception errors affect an autonomous vehicle’s driving decisions. This paper develops a framework for evaluating perception through its consequences for planning. The central question is how errors in the estimated world state change the decision process that actually controls the vehicle.

The authors express planning as expected-utility maximization. Signals from upstream modules jointly describe the world, and the planner chooses an action according to a utility determined by both that world state and the action. This formulation connects the quality of perception inputs to the objective used when selecting vehicle behavior.

Under practical conditions, the objective can be written as an inner product between a world-state description and a utility function in a Hilbert space. That geometric representation enables analysis of how world-estimation noise affects planning and leads to a proposed universal perception metric. The contribution is a principled connection between perception error and planning utility, with the geometric result depending on the conditions established in the paper.
icml-2023-transcendental-idealism-of-pla.tldr: The paper derives a geometric framework and perception metric that assess autonomous-driving perception errors through their effects on planning utility.
